tagline.text: A pink heritage house on Silay's main road showing life in the sugar era

location.label: Location
location.text: Rizal St., Silay City, Negros Occidental

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱250–700 (Silay day trip from Bacolod, including admission, transport and food)

children.text: Known as the Pink House for its pink walls, the Bernardino Jalandoni Museum is a two-storey mansion completed in 1908 and the first National Historical Landmark in Silay. With a guide you can see carriages, a Steinway piano and German ceiling panels that show how a sugar baron's household lived.

The Bernardino Jalandoni Museum (the Bernardino and Ysabel Jalandoni Ancestral House) is a lifestyle museum on Rizal Street in Silay City, Negros Occidental. Its eye-catching pink walls earn it the local name "Pink House," and it is said to have been completed in
. The Jalandonis came from Jaro in Iloilo and settled in Silay, where they raised their children in this house. On
November 6, 1993

the National Historical Institute declared it a National Historical Landmark, described as the first in Silay to be so recognized. A marker from the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) stands just outside the front door.

The house is a two-storey bahay na bato, described as a larger-scale version of the traditional bahay kubo. The posts and floors use balayong hardwood shipped from Mindoro, and the ceiling carries embossed steel panels brought from Hamburg, Germany. Large windows use capiz shells instead of glass, which gives privacy while letting in light and air, and the transoms above the doors have cut-out callado tracery with a French-influenced design. A story is also told that when the main road was widened, residents fought to protect the heritage houses, so the street in front stayed narrower than the rest.

The visit begins on the ground floor, in the former garage. Carts, a horse carriage and a caromata stand there, and one account mentions a carroza (festival float) carrying a statue of the Virgin Mary that is still paraded through town during Holy Week, as well as the family's doll collection and old photographs of Silay and Manila. Upstairs, the living room, bedrooms, kitchen, dining room and study follow one another, with everyday objects such as a Steinway piano, a gramophone, a sewing machine, an old telephone, four-poster beds, chamber pots and a birthing chair. The kitchen has heavy chopping blocks called prinsa de paa and prinsa de mano, along with round irons.

The house was inherited by a descendant, Antonio Montinola, and its care is entrusted to the Silay Heritage Foundation. It is also used for arts, cultural and educational events and performances. The Hofileña Ancestral House and Balay Negrense stand close by on the same side of town, so the Pink House is most often visited as one stop on the Silay heritage walk that links the three. One traveler who walked every street on a heritage map from the airport counted more than 20 large mansions, yet only three open their interiors to the public. That makes the Pink House a rare chance to see inside. The second-floor displays center on furniture from the era when sugar was the city's main product, with rocking chairs, chandeliers, large tables and dressers, and old-world beds that show how a wealthy family lived.

blocks.title: Pink exterior and the landmark marker

children.text: The pink walls stand out even from the main road and make the first impression. The house was declared a national landmark in
, and the NHCP marker is outside the front door. One account gives a board resolution dated
April 6
of the same year, so the declaration date differs a little between sources.

blocks.title: Carriages in the old ground-floor garage

children.text: The garage layout common in 1900s mansions has been preserved. Carriages, carts and a bench with a chicken coop underneath (a gallinera) are on display, and the cool, high space is a pleasant place to rest first on a hot day.

The ceiling panels were brought from Hamburg, Germany, and each carries a pattern. The balayong hardwood of the floors and posts is said to have been shipped from Mindoro, which gives a sense of the scale of materials a sugar baron could source.
Large windows fitted with capiz shells instead of glass let in soft light. Callado tracery above the rooms helps air circulate and also serves as decoration.

blocks.title: Steinway piano and gramophone in the living room

children.text: The upstairs living room holds a Steinway piano, a gramophone, a sewing machine, an old telephone and paintings. One visitor wrote that a wooden harp and family portraits covered the walls. Displays can change, so check on site.

Four-poster beds, chamber pots and a birthing chair stand in the bedrooms. Imported household goods of the time, such as an ice box and a water filter, are also mentioned, so you can imagine the daily life of the upper class in the sugar boom in concrete detail.
There are thick wooden chopping blocks called prinsa de paa and prinsa de mano, and round irons heated with fire. The kitchen stories are more fun when the guide explains how each item was used.

blocks.title: Upstairs veranda and the guide's anecdotes

children.text: The veranda at the back of the second floor is described as a spot to rest while looking down at an old tamarind tree. The guide often leads the tour for about
1 hour
, adding anecdotes about each object, what happened in each room and the people who lived there.

items.title: Silay heritage walk
items.subtitle: A half day centered on the Pink House

children.text: Travel north from Bacolod for about
30 minutes to 1 hour
to reach Silay. By public transport, take a bus bound for Victorias from the Bacolod North Terminal and get off in Silay.

Have a pie and coffee for breakfast at El Ideal bakery. One visitor recommended its guapple pie and buko pie and wrote that the staff kept their heavy backpacks for them. Another account says the Pink House is about a
1 minute
walk away.

Take a guided tour of the Bernardino Jalandoni Museum soon after it opens. After the ground-floor garage, carriages, dolls and photographs, go through the second-floor living room, bedrooms, kitchen and dining room in turn.

Walk toward Cinco de Noviembre Street to see the Hofileña Ancestral House and Balay Negrense. Visitors say admission to all three is similar, but check on site whether they are closed or under restoration.
Have lunch while walking past San Diego Pro-Cathedral and the old houses of the town center.
Return to Bacolod to rest, or have dinner at a seaside restaurant.
By accounts from the 2010s, the museum opens Tuesday to Saturday from 9 to 5 and Sunday from 9 to 4. It is known to close on Mondays, but check the latest announcement.
Take a domestic flight from Manila to Bacolod-Silay Airport (BCD). Carriers and times change by season, so check with the airline.
The airport lies within Silay, and from the main gate you can take a tricycle downtown. In a 2013 report it cost about
, though it is often higher now.
From downtown you walk to the museum.
Take a bus bound for Victorias from the Bacolod North Terminal and get off in Silay. In a 2013 report the bus fare was
, and it may be higher now.
You can also go by taxi or ride-hailing car. The travel time varies with traffic.
Some operators run Silay heritage tour packages that include hotel pickup.
The museum sits on Rizal Street along the main road, close to El Ideal bakery.
You can walk to the Hofileña Ancestral House and Balay Negrense toward Cinco de Noviembre Street.
On hot days take a tricycle, but agree on the fare first.
Since the visit is mostly indoors, weather matters little, but if you want to walk between several houses, the dry season of
December–May
is more comfortable. To avoid the midday heat, visit soon after opening.
Bacolod's MassKara Festival takes place in
October
and the city is crowded, so secure lodging and transport in advance. Visitors say weekday afternoons are relatively quiet.

Most people visit Silay as a day trip and book their lodging in Bacolod. Bacolod has a wide choice of hotels and restaurants, which makes it a good place for dinner after the house tour.

In Silay, El Ideal bakery is the most famous stop. Its guapple pie and buko (coconut) pie come up often in accounts, and it makes a good breakfast and rest stop before or after the museum. Hours can change, so check on the day. Visitors also mention cafes set in old houses in town, and in Bacolod, Negros chicken inasal and sweet snacks are well loved.
Visiting soon after opening is quiet and cool, so it is easier to follow the guide's explanations.
Accounts say the tour takes close to an hour, so leave room in your schedule.
During Holy Week the Virgin Mary float from the ground floor is used in the town procession, so a visit then may coincide with a Silay tradition. Check local announcements for the schedule.
The guide tells anecdotes, so ask questions and offer a tip at the end as a courtesy.
Some accounts say photos are taken without flash. Ask the guide about the rules before you begin.
Only three of Silay's heritage houses are open to the public, so plan them together rather than rushing at one.
Visitors report that El Ideal bakery and similar places sometimes keep heavy bags, but this is not guaranteed.
Check closing days and hours in advance by phone or social media.

The usual route starts in the ground-floor garage and moves upstairs, and accounts say the tour ends on the veranda at the end of the second floor. From the veranda you can look out toward where sugarcane fields once stood.
Admission and opening hours differ by source, and most come from accounts in the 2010s. Check local announcements before you go.
Admission reports range from ₱25 to ₱150. Go by the notice on site.
It is known to close on Mondays, but this may change with holidays and events.
This is an old wooden building, so watch your step on the stairs and floors to avoid slipping, and do not touch the exhibits.
Balay Negrense may be closed for restoration, which could throw off a plan to visit all three houses.
When the house is booked for an event, some areas may be restricted.
Known as the "Paris of Negros," this heritage city gathers ancestral house museums, a cathedral and bakeries.
Silay
is a pleasant place to explore on foot.
This cathedral in the center of town fits naturally into the heritage walk route.
These are the ruins of a sugar baron's mansion in Talisay. They are roughly
10 km
from Silay, so check how you will get there.
The central city of Negros Occidental, with lodging, restaurants and downtown sights.
